titel: Forever chemicals are hiding everywhere. These five habits can help you avoid them. (From the archives)
einzeiler: How forever chemicals spread worldwide and what you can do to avoid them
kurzfassung: Investigative journalist Mariah Blake discusses the widespread contamination of forever chemicals, or PFAS, tracing their origins back to the Manhattan Project. She explains how major chemical companies concealed toxicity data for decades while the compounds infiltrated everyday consumer products and drinking water sources. Finally, she shares practical steps individuals can take to reduce their personal exposure and highlights growing grassroots activism.
stichpunkte: Forever chemicals, or PFAS, are synthetic compounds prized for resisting heat, water, and grease, but they persist in the environment for thousands of years.
The U.S. government originally developed these chemicals during the Manhattan Project to handle caustic materials for uranium enrichment.
Internal documents from manufacturers like 3M and DuPont reveal they knew about the severe health risks and blood accumulation since the 1960s and 1970s.
A lawsuit by a West Virginia farming family exposed a major cover-up and triggered a large study linking PFAS to six serious diseases.
Regulators historically lagged behind because chemical laws grandfathered in existing substances, leaving oversight extremely weak.
Grassordinary citizens in places like Hoosick Falls, New York, sparked a nationwide movement by testing their water and demanding accountability.
State-level bans, thousands of lawsuits, and pledges from major retailers are driving a massive shift away from PFAS use.
Individuals can protect themselves by filtering drinking water, avoiding stain-resistant items, and skipping locally caught freshwater fish.

clips.text: An industry document estimated that the persistence of a single forever chemical spans one million years.

clips.hook: An aborted study on lab animals
clips.text: Early laboratory research involving monkeys had to be canceled prematurely because every single test subject died.
A homeowner who saved up for her dream house discovered her body contained PFAS concentrations comparable to individuals who handled the chemicals professionally for decades.

clips.hook: Markets move fast while regulation crawls
clips.text: Economic forces and liability pressures drive corporate change much faster than government oversight ever could.

clips.hook: The hidden danger in a single fish
clips.text: Consuming one portion of locally caught freshwater fish can raise a person's internal chemical levels as much as drinking polluted water for a whole month.

beschreibung:
This is an episode from our archives. It originally aired in May 2025.

Forever chemicals, also known as PFAS, are found in virtually every corner of the world, including in most people’s bodies. These synthetic compounds have been linked to a wide range of health issues — from infertility to cancer to neurological problems — even at low levels of exposure. In a new book, They Poisoned the World: Life and Death in the Age of Forever Chemicals, investigative journalist Mariah Blake lays out how these toxic chemicals became so ubiquitous. Blake spoke with Apple News In Conversation host Shumita Basu about a group of unlikely activists fighting back against those responsible and offers practical tips to protect yourself.
